theorem_conditions.location: L1. Reduction of the signs of the integer anchors
theorem_conditions.conditions: Two nonzero integer elements of opposite signs belong to a D(1) tuple.
theorem_conditions.assessment: The product is an integer at most -1, while product plus 1 being a rational square forces the product to be at least -1. Thus the product is -1 and the pair is {-1,1}. Negation preserves all pairwise products. For that exceptional pair, any other element x has 1+x and 1-x nonnegative, hence -1 <= x <= 1; distinctness excludes the endpoints, and the only integer strictly between them is zero, which is forbidden. The reduction is sound and does not imply the remaining elements are positive.

theorem_conditions.claim: L2 common-neighbor parametrization and K4 reformulation
theorem_conditions.location: L2. Complete rational parametrization of common neighbors
theorem_conditions.conditions: a,b are distinct nonzero rationals; x is a nonzero rational common neighbor; for the K4 statement additionally ab+1 is a rational square.
theorem_conditions.assessment: The formulas satisfy both square equations by expansion. In the converse, u=±1 would force x=0. With t=(v-1)/(u-1), substitution gives (u-1)[(b-at^2)(u-1)+2(b-at)]=0. The stated excluded case b=at^2 forces b=at, hence t=1 and a=b, a contradiction; solving then yields the displayed formulas. Every such x therefore has a finite parameter t. Four distinct common neighbors pairwise adjacent are exactly the four additional elements needed with a,b for a sextuple, so the infinite-graph K4 equivalence holds. A bounded parameter search is only a finite induced subgraph.

theorem_conditions.location: L3. Denominator support and its limitation
theorem_conditions.conditions: a,b are distinct nonzero integers; x=u/v is reduced with v>0 and is a common neighbor.
theorem_conditions.assessment: The gcd identity gcd(au+v,v)=gcd(a,v) gives the reduced denominator v/gcd(a,v) for ax+1. A reduced rational square has square numerator and denominator, including the zero-square case, so this quotient is a square; likewise for b. The valuation parity condition follows. The coprime-anchor conclusion is properly conditional. The supplied example is arithmetically consistent: 12943=7*43^2, and the two square values have numerators 47^2 and 137^2 over 43^2 after reduction as stated. It demonstrates why the coprimality condition matters.

theorem_conditions.claim: L4 obstruction for the canonical order-three point
theorem_conditions.location: L4. The canonical order-three seed cannot contain two integers
theorem_conditions.conditions: a,b,c are distinct nonzero rationals forming a D(1) triple; S=(1,R) on the specified curve has order exactly 3; for the contradiction, two of a,b,c are integers.
theorem_conditions.assessment: The symmetric sums give the stated cubic and R^2. The tangent slope is (3+2V+Uz)/(2R); because 2S=-S, the doubling x-coordinate condition is lambda^2=V+3, yielding the stated equation T=0. The two displayed identities then imply 1+z^2 is a rational square because R is nonzero. Substituting U=A+z/B and V=B+Az/B into T=0 gives the displayed monic integer quartic (its coefficients agree on expansion). The rational-root theorem forces z to be an integer; z is nonzero, and z^2<z^2+1<(abs(z)+1)^2 contradicts its being an integer square. This proves only the stated obstruction for this canonical point and triple; it does not cover other coordinate placements in a sextuple.

theorem_conditions.claim: L5 degenerate family in the preliminary extension equation
theorem_conditions.location: L5. A whole family of false positives in the quadruple extension test
theorem_conditions.conditions: Integer s>=2 and the specified a,b,c,d. The claim concerns the stated preliminary identity and extension equation, not all possible extensions of the quadruple.
theorem_conditions.assessment: The six listed square roots square to the corresponding pairwise products plus one. The stated linear term in the extension equation is zero, the right-hand product is zero, and abcd-1=-2(b-1)^2/b is nonzero; hence the equation forces x=0. The scope limitation is essential: this only shows that this equation's appended roots degenerate, not that the quadruple has no other rational extensions.
